notes.meaning: God tells His people to mark the month of Abib and keep the Passover each year. Abib was the spring month when the barley harvest began, and God made it the start of their religious year. They were to remember that God rescued them from Egypt in the night, when Pharaoh finally gave them permission to leave.

Israel was to offer the Passover sacrifices at the one central place of worship God would select. While the main Passover meal required a young lamb or goat, larger animals from the herd were offered for the feast days that followed. Bringing these sacrifices to the central sanctuary reminded them that God dwelt among His gathered people.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many historical-critical scholars view this command for a single altar as reflecting reforms under King Josiah centuries later, rather than instructions spoken directly by Moses.

notes.meaning: The people were told to eat bread made without yeast for seven full days. This flat bread is called the bread of affliction because it tasted plain and reminded them of their hard slavery. It also recalled how hurriedly they fled Egypt, without even enough time to let their dough rise.

No yeast was allowed anywhere in the homes of Israel during the week of the feast. In addition, all the meat sacrificed on the first evening had to be eaten that night, leaving none for the morning. This kept the sacred food fresh and honoured God's original instructions for the night of their rescue.

The Passover could no longer be killed in any local town or private home as it was back in Egypt. Instead, the people had to travel to the central place chosen by God for His name to dwell. The sacrifice took place at sunset, marking the exact time of day when they first prepared to leave Egyptian slavery.

The worshipers were to cook and eat the Passover meal at the central sanctuary site. When morning came, they were free to go back to their temporary camps and lodgings. They could then complete the rest of the week's celebration near the sanctuary.

Bread without yeast was eaten through the six days that followed the initial Passover evening. On the seventh day, the whole community gathered for a sacred assembly dedicated to the Lord. Regular daily work stopped so everyone could focus entirely on worshipping God.

Israel was instructed to count seven full weeks starting from the day they first cut the ripe barley with a sickle. This span of fifty days connected the spring harvest directly to their next major national celebration. It showed that both the grain and their daily bread came from God's hand.

At the end of the seven weeks, the people kept the Feast of Weeks, also called Pentecost. Each family brought a voluntary offering based on how richly the Lord had provided for them that season. Those who were blessed with a larger harvest gave generously from a grateful heart.

The Feast of Weeks was designed to be a time of shared gladness before God at His chosen sanctuary. Landowners were commanded to include their children, servants, local Levites, foreigners, orphans, and widows in the festive meals. God wanted those with few resources to share fully in the celebration.

God reminded the Israelites that they were once helpless slaves in the land of Egypt. Remembering their own humble past was meant to keep them tender toward the needy and eager to obey God's laws. True thankfulness for rescue shows itself in obedience and kindness.

The Feast of Tabernacles, or Shelters, lasted for seven days in the autumn. It took place after all the grain was threshed and all the grapes were pressed into wine. The feast celebrated the completed harvest and remembered how God sheltered their ancestors during their years wandering in the desert.

This autumn feast was filled with great public rejoicing. Just like the Feast of Weeks, the celebration was not kept to oneself, but shared with family, servants, Levites, and the vulnerable poor. Everyone was welcomed to taste the goodness of God's abundant provision.

For an entire week the people gathered at the place chosen by God to celebrate His faithfulness. Because the Lord had blessed their crops and everyday labour, their joy was to be full and deep. Remembering God's gifts gives His people real and lasting happiness.

Every adult male was required to travel to the central place of worship three times each year for these major feasts. Women and children often came along, but the men had the legal duty to represent their households. None of them was to arrive before the Lord with empty hands.

Each worshiper gave a gift according to his ability, matching the degree to which God had blessed him. God did not demand the same amount from everyone, but looked for a willing, honest return based on what a person had received. Giving back to God is a normal part of worship.

Israel was instructed to appoint judges and court officers in every town throughout all the tribes. In Bible times, trials and public business took place at the open area near the city gates. These local leaders were charged to govern and decide legal disputes with strict fairness.

Judges were strictly forbidden from bending the law, favouring rich or influential friends, or taking bribes. Secret payments ruin clear judgment and cause even wise and honest people to make crooked rulings. Leaders must treat every person by the same honest standard.

Moses repeated the word justice to show that pure fairness must be pursued with total dedication. The nation's ability to thrive and remain safely in the promised land depended on upright courts. When a society loves fairness, God protects and blesses it.

The people were forbidden from planting a wooden pole or grove dedicated to the Canaanite goddess Asherah near God's altar. Surrounding nations used shaded groves and wooden carvings for corrupt pagan rites. God wanted His worship kept purely public, clear of all idolatrous customs.

Israel was also told never to set up a sacred stone pillar for worship, because the Lord despises such things. Neighbouring peoples carved and set up stone pillars in honour of false gods like Baal. The true God is an eternal Spirit who must never be represented by lifeless stone.
